ratings.plot: Things go wrong for a high ranking mobster when he doesn't follow his boss's orders.

verdict.reason: Kim Jee-woon's crime masterpiece deserves a theater. The DCP restoration at Metrograph makes the violent elegance sing.

ratings.plot: Ryuichi Sakamoto's last performance, a concert film featuring just him and his piano playing for the last time before passing away.

verdict.reason: Watch Sakamoto's final concert on the big screen at Metrograph. It's a rare, intimate document of an irreplaceable artist at the piano.

ratings.plot: In Mumbai, Nurse Prabha's routine is troubled when she receives an unexpected gift from her estranged husband. Her younger roommate, Anu, tries in vain to find a spot in the city to be intimate with her boyfriend.

verdict.reason: Watch it. Kapadia's debut is a precise, patient film about two women in Mumbai finding small moments of freedom, shot with rare visual clarity on 35mm.

ratings.plot: In the twilight of Francisco Franco's dictatorship, an 8-year-old orphan and her two sisters find shelter in the house of their stern aunt and try their best to acclimatize to a new reality. Can they summon up the courage to grow up?

verdict.reason: A masterpiece of post-Franco Spanish cinema demands to be seen on film. Metrograph's 35mm print restores Saura's precise control of light and shadow to their full force.

ratings.plot: A traveling psychic who helps lost souls cross over encounters a powerful entity at a remote house. While investigating its origins, she uncovers dark secrets and faces a deadly threat from an unexpected source.

verdict.reason: A confident debut from Dave Boyle with genuine scares and a strong central performance. The house itself becomes a character, and the final act twist lands hard.

ratings.plot: A thorough and unvarnished analysis of Elon Musk, a technology billionaire who serves as the CEO of Tesla, SpaceX, and Twitter.

verdict.reason: Gibney brings his investigative rigor to a figure who demands scrutiny. The access and unvarnished framing make this essential viewing on a big screen.

ratings.plot: A hard-partying New York City club promoter sees his whirlwind lifestyle upended by the arrival of the 10-year-old son he never knew he had.

verdict.reason: Jordan Firstman's debut is sharp comedy about reinvention in New York's party scene. See it at Lincoln Center before word spreads and it vanishes.

ratings.plot: Misael lives as an independent logger in the woods, enjoying his solitary freedom. When he must care for his older sister, his peaceful existence is upended and the foundations of his carefully constructed life begin to fall apart.

verdict.reason: Lisandro Alonso's meditative work on solitude and obligation deserves the big screen. A 100-minute Lincoln Center screening of a director working at full precision.

ratings.plot: Follows a mother, her daughter, and a teenage boy blamed for a tragic death as they travel to Tenerife together, confronting grief, blame, and forgiveness on a family holiday that never happened.

verdict.reason: Sandra Wollner's chamber drama about grief and blame deserves the theater. The 121-minute runtime and intimate character work demand full attention on a big screen.

ratings.plot: A glimpse at the lives of two petty criminals in Taipei.

verdict.reason: Hou Hsiao-hsien's 1996 masterpiece demands a theater and a full two hours of attention. The 116-minute rhythm and Taipei street photography are built for the big screen.

movies.title: Once Upon a Time in Harlem

ratings.plot: A decade post-death, filmmaker William Greaves reveals his final work: footage of a 1972 gathering he arranged with Harlem Renaissance legends, which he deemed his most significant capture.

verdict.reason: A lost Greaves documentary surfaces with pristine restoration at Lincoln Center. Rare archival footage of Harlem Renaissance figures in 1972 makes this essential cinema history.

ratings.plot: Four strangers' paths cross by chance, leading to complex emotional entanglements that challenge their existing relationships and force them to confront uncomfortable truths about love and commitment.

verdict.reason: Lee Chang-dong's first film in a decade demands the big screen and your full attention. Nearly three hours of moral complexity and emotional precision—see it before word spreads.

ratings.plot: A criminal on the run hides in a circus and seeks to possess the daughter of the ringmaster at any cost.

verdict.reason: Browning's 1927 masterpiece of obsession and circus grotesquerie belongs on the big screen. Silent cinema at this level of visual invention demands the theater.

ratings.plot: In secret conversations on the rooftops of Tel Aviv at night, the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza are revealed by the people who designed and operated them.

verdict.reason: Essential testimony from the people who built Israel's targeting systems, shot in the dark on Tel Aviv rooftops. The 80-minute runtime keeps the weight intact without padding.

ratings.plot: The foundations of Grayson Manor are shaken when an accident leaves Boyd Grayson handless and his mother invests in radical new technology to help him.

verdict.reason: Glenn McQuaid's perfect-scored horror film about body horror and maternal obsession demands a theater. The restored print at Alamo Drafthouse is the only way to see it tonight.

ratings.plot: Thirty-four days before she’s sent to prison, notorious Silicon Valley founder Elizabeth Holmes invites a skeptical film crew to document her every move. What begins as an intimate portrait of an enigmatic felon becomes a mind-bending three-year journey into the abyss. From boundary-pushing directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim comes YOU CAN SEE EVERYTHING.

verdict.reason: Nathan Fielding and Lance Oppenheim have made something genuinely disorienting about power, performance, and the camera's complicity—a three-hour document that earns its runtime. The film's structural ambition (letting Holmes control her own image while the filmmakers undermine it) is best experienced on the big screen where the manipulation becomes tactile.

ratings.plot: Cameron Winter, in December 2025, after a months-long sold-out tour with his band Geese, returned to New York to play a single show at Carnegie Hall. This is the movie. Directed and shot on 35mm and 16mm by Oscar-winning filmmaker Paul Thomas Anderson (ONE BATTLE AFTER ANOTHER), the crew includes filmmaker and actor Benny Safdie (THE SMASHING MACHINE) and music producer Ariel Rechtshaid (Grammy winner for albums with Vampire Weekend and Adele). GQ praised Cameron Winter’s show at Carnegie Hall as “staggeringly good,” and Nick Cave said he has "a glorious, emotive voice with brilliant, blistering words, a racked and wondrous thing.” Winter’s solo album Heavy Metal was named one of the best of the year by Pitchfork , Rolling Stone , Paste , and Mojo , and Geese’s last record Getting Killed was named the best album of 2025 by The New Yorker , NME , and Stereogum .

verdict.reason: Paul Thomas Anderson shot a 72-minute concert film on 35mm and 16mm—go for the image alone. Winter's voice and songwriting merit the big screen, and this is the only way to see it.

ratings.plot: An enduring, singular masterpiece of cinema starring Academy Award®-winner Vanessa Redgrave and Oliver Reed, KEN RUSSELL’S THE DEVILS is a prescient epic of obsession and corruption, and a defining work of art from seminal filmmaker Ken Russell. Assembled from the original camera negative, this new 4K restoration presents Ken Russell’s definitive vision of THE DEVILS by referencing the edit he privately constructed in 2004. KEN RUSSELL’S THE DEVILS is the uncut and unfiltered theatrical experience that Russell always envisioned – and the first time, the film will be presented restored and in 4K.

verdict.reason: Russell's uncompromising vision of obsession and corruption deserves the big screen. This 4K restoration from the original negative finally presents his definitive cut in full.

ratings.plot: Soon after a stranger arrives in a little village, a mysterious sickness starts spreading. A policeman, drawn into the incident, is forced to solve the mystery in order to save his daughter...

verdict.reason: A rare theatrical return of Na Hong-jin's masterwork—mystery and dread that deepens with every viewing. The 156-minute runtime demands a big screen and Metrograph's DCP projection.

ratings.plot: A portrait of genius music composer Ryuichi Sakamoto.

verdict.reason: A rare theatrical screening of one of the essential music documentaries of the decade. Schible captures Sakamoto's final creative period with intimate access and formal sophistication that demands a big screen and proper sound.

movies.title: The Taking of Pelham One Two Three

ratings.plot: Four armed men hijack a New York City subway car and demand a ransom for the passengers. The city's police are faced with a conundrum: Even if it's paid, how could they get away?

verdict.reason: See this '70s masterclass in procedural tension on the big screen. The 35mm print at Metrograph restores every detail of the subway car and the city streets above it.

ratings.plot: A high-strung news producer finds herself in a love triangle between a talented but self-doubting reporter and a charming new anchor, who embodies the growing trivialization of news that she is determined to fight against.

verdict.reason: One of the sharpest films about journalism, ambition, and the cost of principle — see it restored at Metrograph while it plays. Holly Hunter's performance is a masterclass in conveying intelligence and heartbreak through restraint.

ratings.plot: A psychopath tries to forcibly persuade a tennis star to agree to his theory that two strangers can get away with murder by submitting to his plan to kill the other's most-hated person.

verdict.reason: Hitchcock's masterpiece of psychological manipulation deserves the big screen. The 35mm print at Metrograph shows why the geometry of his shot-making still cuts.

ratings.plot: An executive of a Yokohama shoe company becomes a victim of extortion when his chauffeur's son is kidnapped by mistake and held for ransom.

verdict.reason: One of Kurosawa's masterworks about class and moral choice—see it on 35mm at Metrograph. The cinematography and structural precision demand the big screen.

ratings.plot: Portrait of a middle-class family in Taipei. A man in his forties, his teenage daughter and his eight-year-old son experience life, navigating between remorse, hope and disappointment.

verdict.reason: Worth the trip for Edward Yang's three-hour masterpiece on family life and time's passage. Metrograph's DCP restoration honors the precision of Yang's composition and color.

ratings.plot: A young woman suspects her neighbors have sinister plans for her pregnancy.

verdict.reason: One of cinema's great paranoia films—see it on 35mm at Metrograph. Polanski's control of suspense and Mia Farrow's performance define the modern horror picture.

ratings.plot: A filmmaker applies lessons from a Hallmark movie writing workshop to pitch a documentary about concrete.

verdict.reason: John Wilson's deadpan absurdism makes even a concrete doc sing. A perfect 100-minute palate cleanser about nothing and everything at once.

ratings.plot: The story of Danish soldier and explorer Ludvig Kahlen, who explored and cultivated Denmark's wild Jutland, which now comprises the vast majority of the country, in the mid-18th century.

verdict.reason: Arcel's 18th-century Danish epic plays like a frontier film with genuine historical weight. Film Forum's presentation honors the scale and detail of his landscape cinematography.

ratings.plot: Direct continuation of Takashi Yamazaki's Godzilla Minus One.

verdict.reason: Takashi Yamazaki returns to finish what he started—essential for anyone who saw Minus One. A 119-minute continuation from the director of that film demands the big screen.

ratings.plot: Fifteen years after murdering his sister on Halloween night 1963, Michael Myers escapes from a mental hospital and returns to the small town of Haddonfield, Illinois, to kill again.

verdict.reason: Carpenter's lean, methodical filmmaking defined the slasher template and still works as pure cinema. Ninety-one minutes of sustained dread—every frame counts, no fat.

ratings.plot: A research chemist comes under personal and professional attack when he decides to appear in a 60 Minutes exposé on Big Tobacco.

verdict.reason: Mann's corporate thriller holds up as essential political cinema. Metrograph is screening it on 35mm, the format that captures his obsessive cinematography.

ratings.plot: Self-doubt, sacrifice and struggle converge into an existential crisis for a devoted classical vocalist as the mastery he strives for remains elusive.

verdict.reason: A rare New York screening of Tamhane's austere masterpiece about classical music and spiritual doubt. The 129-minute runtime and chamber intimacy demand the theater's focus.

movies.title: Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother

ratings.plot: Follows Latif, a devoutly religious hitman, who embarks on a desperate journey across Houston to protect his children after his wife dies, confronting forces closing in and beliefs threatening to unravel.

verdict.reason: Watch it; Tariq brings real stakes to a hitman's moral crisis across Houston. The 35mm print at Angelika or Empire rewards the film's visual intensity on a big screen.

ratings.plot: As World War II and the German occupation ends, the Polish resistance and the Soviet forces turn on each other in an attempt to take over leadership in Communist Poland.

verdict.reason: One of the essential Polish films—see Wajda's masterpiece about resistance and betrayal on a big screen at Film Forum. The final sequence alone justifies the trip.

ratings.plot: Odysseus, king of Ithaca, embarks on a perilous journey to return home after the Trojan War.

verdict.reason: Nolan on a 172-minute epic in 70mm is worth the trip. Catch it in the largest format available—the theatrical scale is the whole point.

ratings.plot: A group of high school students sets off on a school trip to discover the ruins of Pompeii. They are seized by a sense of vertigo. They allow themselves to be overwhelmed by desire and anger, until they surrender completely.

verdict.reason: A rare debut that justifies the hype—Pompeii's ruins become a stage for teenage vertigo and desire. Atlan's control of mood and image demands the big screen at Lincoln Center.

ratings.plot: After enduring years of malfunctioning products, Wile E. Coyote teams up with a local personal injury attorney to take on ACME, the manufacturer of anything and everything used by the Looney Tunes characters.

verdict.reason: Worth the trip for a Looney Tunes film that actually lands the joke. Dave Green finds real comedy in the lawsuit premise instead of coasting on nostalgia.

ratings.plot: Follows a hapless courier tasked with delivering a package to a remote hospital. He soon finds himself caught in the middle of an outbreak and must fight through hordes of mutated creatures to survive.

verdict.reason: Zach Cregger brings sharp genre instincts to a survival premise that plays for laughs and scares. The 90-minute runtime keeps the action lean and means you're home before midnight.

ratings.plot: A modern adaptation of the classic Greek tragedy which falls within a social realism. To the law of men, the young Antigone apposes her own sets of values.

verdict.reason: A rare 35mm screening of a vital contemporary rereading of Sophocles that refuses easy answers. Deraspe's social realism cuts deeper than the source material's abstractions.

ratings.plot: Meeting a stranger in a railway station, a woman is tempted to cheat on her husband.

verdict.reason: One of the great films about desire and restraint—see Lean's precision on 35mm at Metrograph. The restored print makes every glance and hesitation cut like glass.

ratings.plot: At Westerburg High where cliques rule, jocks dominate and all the popular girls are named Heather, it's going to take a Veronica and mysterious new kid to give teen angst a body count.

verdict.reason: One of the sharpest satires of American high school ever made—caustic, funny, and structurally airtight in ways most comedies aren't. Metrograph's DCP restoration lets you see the production design and framing that make Lehmann's staging as precise as the script.

ratings.plot: "The Washington Post" reporters Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein uncover the details of the Watergate scandal that leads to President Richard Nixon's resignation.

verdict.reason: Essential political thriller that defined the genre and still moves like a freight train. Metrograph's DCP restoration lets you see the craftsmanship in every frame.

ratings.plot: In an increasingly Westernized postwar Tokyo, an aging widower arranges a marriage for his only daughter.

verdict.reason: Ozu's final film is essential—a masterwork of stillness and domestic grace at a major venue. Metrograph's DCP restoration lets you see the precise geometry of every frame.

ratings.plot: In 19th century Massachusetts, the March sisters--Meg, Jo, Beth, and Amy--on the threshold of womanhood, go through many ups and downs in life and endeavor to make important decisions about their futures.

verdict.reason: Gerwig's take on this story justifies the trip, especially on Metrograph's screen. The 135-minute runtime and formal precision reward theatrical attention.

ratings.plot: When a nobleman is threatened by a family curse on his newly inherited estate, detective Sherlock Holmes is hired to investigate.

verdict.reason: Terence Fisher's 1959 take is the definitive Sherlock adaptation on screen. Metrograph's DCP restoration makes this the night to catch it.

movies.title: If I Go Will They Miss Me

ratings.plot: A boy sees ghostly figures of other boys in his neighborhood while grappling with his father's distance. These visions uncover hidden connections between them and their shared heritage.

verdict.reason: A rare debut feature that uses magical realism to explore fatherhood and Black identity with real depth. Thompson-Hernandez's control of image and tone justifies the trip.
A rare screening at Lincoln Center of a film with near-universal praise. See it on the big screen while you can.

ratings.plot: A woman who agrees to a deal to help an old acquaintance. She follows the hero on his adventure and enters dangerous territory where she is then confronted with her own desire.

verdict.reason: Grisebach's first action film earns top marks for direction and visual ambition. Lincoln Center is the right venue for a 167-minute work that privileges image over plot momentum.

ratings.plot: Two best friends become stranded on the mystical world of Nakali, where their only escape might cost them their shared lifetime of memories.

verdict.reason: Skip the streaming queue and catch this one theatrically—the animation design demands a big screen and the emotional core about friendship and sacrifice lands harder in a theater full of people. The 109-minute runtime moves fast enough to hold attention, and the world-building rewards the full theatrical experience.

ratings.plot: To satisfy his nagging parents, a gay landlord and a female tenant agree to a marriage of convenience, but his parents arrive to visit and things get out of hand.

verdict.reason: Ang Lee's debut is a smart comedy that earns its emotional turns without losing its edge. Metrograph is showing it on 35mm.

movies.title: Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown

ratings.plot: A television actress encounters a variety of eccentric characters after embarking on a journey to discover why her lover abruptly left her.

verdict.reason: Essential Almodóvar on 35mm at Metrograph. The 1988 restoration glows on film; this is how the color and rhythm were meant to land.

movies.title: The Flavor of Green Tea Over Rice

ratings.plot: A childless middle-aged couple faces a marital crisis.

verdict.reason: Essential Ozu on 35mm at Metrograph. A masterwork about marriage and compromise that demands the big screen.

ratings.plot: After the devastating events of Avengers: Infinity War (2018), the universe is in ruins. With the help of remaining allies, the Avengers assemble once more in order to reverse Thanos' actions and restore balance to the universe.

verdict.reason: Three hours well spent on a spectacle designed for the big screen. IMAX or 4DX amplifies the final battle sequences that justify the runtime.

movies.title: Once Upon a Time in China II

ratings.plot: Arriving by train in Guangzhou, 1895, the trio fight off White Lotus followers, who want to kill all foreigners and the cute, European dressed 13th Aunt. It's not kung fu master Dr. Wong's (Jet Li) last fight.

verdict.reason: Tsui Hark's action cinema at full throttle belongs on the big screen. Jet Li's physical precision and the film's kinetic editing make this a rare theatrical event worth the trip.

ratings.plot: While on a trip to Paris with his fiancée's family, a nostalgic screenwriter finds himself mysteriously going back to the 1920s every day at midnight.

verdict.reason: Allen's best work in years—a romantic fantasy that earns its charm without straining. The 35mm print at Metrograph restores the cinematography to what it should be.

ratings.plot: A bedridden boy's grandfather reads him the story of a farmboy-turned-pirate who encounters numerous obstacles, enemies and allies in his quest to be reunited with his true love.

verdict.reason: A perfect adventure film that works for all ages on the big screen. Rob Reiner balances genuine emotion, comedy, and action without a wasted moment in 98 minutes.

ratings.plot: Arnold Schwarzenegger and Lou Ferrigno face off in a no-holds-barred competition for the title of Mr. Olympia in this critically-acclaimed film that made Schwarzenegger a household name.

verdict.reason: A restoration of the 1977 film that made Schwarzenegger a star deserves the big screen. Metrograph's DCP print lets you see the muscle and ambition in crisp detail.

ratings.plot: An unfinished creation leaves his isolated castle and enters a suburban world eager to embrace him ~ until his differences become impossible to ignore. What begins as a modern fairy tale gradually becomes a story about loneliness,...

verdict.reason: Burton's best film and essential big-screen experience. Metrograph's DCP print restores the precise visual language that defines his entire aesthetic.

ratings.plot: Karsten apparently has it settled. However, in this provincial German town, a moment of weakness turns to disaster, disappointment soon fuels anger, justice hides behind hypocrisy, and evil gradually unfolds.

verdict.reason: A rare screening of this sharp moral thriller at Lincoln Center. Özge traces how a single moment of weakness unravels a man's life in a provincial German town.

ratings.plot: When blues musician Al Cook's memory-filled apartment faces demolition, an old dream emerges from his isolated life.

verdict.reason: Worth the trip to Lincoln Center for a sharp 86-minute drama about memory and loss. A blues musician's fight against demolition carries real weight in this focused character study.

ratings.plot: Explores what it means to be gay throughout different eras, focusing on "three existences" that are connected through themes of sexuality, desire, pain, and inheritance.

verdict.reason: A bold musical spanning eras and sexuality—worth the long runtime for ambitious filmmaking. Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo bring formal invention to intimate material.

ratings.plot: An ostracized fisherwoman commissions the local basketmaker to weave her a husband, but when her wicker creation proves unexpectedly extraordinary, his presence ignites jealousy and upheaval that threatens their quiet village.

verdict.reason: A debut feature that trusts its absurd premise enough to let it breathe—the kind of original fantasy-comedy that belongs on a theater screen, not a laptop. Fischer and Wilson sustain the conceit without winking at it, and the Alamo's crowd-friendly room is the right place to discover something genuinely strange.

ratings.plot: An ambitious loan officer must find a way to shatter a curse that threatens her soul with damnation.

verdict.reason: Sam Raimi at peak form—visceral horror that never loses its dark humor. The practical effects and kinetic camera work demand a theater seat.

ratings.plot: An upper-class widow falls in love with a much younger, down-to-earth nurseryman, much to the disapproval of her children and criticism of her country club peers.

verdict.reason: Sirk's melodrama remains essential—class collision, forbidden desire, and visual depth that only 35mm can deliver. Metrograph's 35mm print is the only way to see this film tonight.

ratings.plot: A high-school boy in the early 1970s is given the chance to write a story for Rolling Stone magazine about an up-and-coming rock band as he accompanies them on their concert tour.

verdict.reason: Crowe's best film about the messy collision of fandom, fame, and growing up deserves the big screen. Metrograph's DCP restoration makes the 1970s rock aesthetic sing.

ratings.plot: An immigrant Romanian family living in Norway is subject to an investigation and faces the scrutiny of the local judicial system.

verdict.reason: Watch it. Mungiu builds juridical pressure with the precision that made 4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days essential—this is a filmmaker at full command.

ratings.plot: When a young boy's family is killed by the mob, their tough neighbor Gloria becomes his reluctant guardian. In possession of a book that the gangsters want, the pair go on the run in New York.

verdict.reason: Cassavetes' kinetic crime thriller demands the big screen and a crowd. Gena Rowlands improvises circles around the mob plot with a performance that defines the film.

ratings.plot: The use of AI technology reaches its most violent and bloody conclusion after a series of deepfake videos are unleashed into the world.

verdict.reason: A sharp horror film about deepfakes that doesn't waste time—90 minutes of escalating dread. Marrs Piliero finds genuine terror in a timely premise without padding.

ratings.plot: A nerdy florist finds his chance for success and romance with the help of a giant man-eating plant who demands to be fed.

verdict.reason: Go to Alamo Drafthouse; Frank Oz's musical comedy belongs in a theater where the fun can breathe. The songs and Rick Moranis's nervy charm demand a crowd.

movies.title: Once Upon a Time in China

ratings.plot: Legendary martial arts hero Wong Fei-Hung fights against foreign forces' plundering of China. When Aunt Yee arrives back from America, Wong Fei-Hung assumes the role of her protector.

verdict.reason: Essential action cinema from Hark Tsui at peak invention. Metrograph's DCP restoration makes the wire work and editing snap with clarity.

ratings.plot: A cyborg assassin from the future attempts to find and kill a young woman who is destined to give birth to a warrior that will lead a resistance to save humankind from extinction.

verdict.reason: Essential action cinema—see it on the big screen at Metrograph. Cameron's control of pace and image design still dominates the room.

ratings.plot: A teenager at Rushmore Academy falls for a much older teacher and befriends a middle-aged industrialist. Later, he finds out that his love interest and his friend are having an affair, which prompts him to begin a vendetta.

verdict.reason: Anderson's deadpan comedy about adolescent obsession holds up perfectly on the big screen. Metrograph is showing the DCP restored, which sharpens every witty frame and musical cue.

ratings.plot: Haru and Luis love competing in Tokyo's ballroom dance scene, but after tragedy strikes, Haru withdraws into isolation. When friends coax her back to the studio, she develops an infatuation with the new instructor.

verdict.reason: A sharp ballroom romance from a strong director about grief and desire. Josef Kubota Wladyka choreographs emotional depth through dance, not just steps.

ratings.plot: A troubled marine seeks to reconcile with the survivors of an Iraqi family he and his unit fired on back in 2003.

verdict.reason: A serious reckoning with American military violence that earns its runtime. Reed Van Dyk directs with the kind of moral weight that demands a theater seat, not a smaller screen.

ratings.plot: Two old friends are walking 600 kilometers through the Scottish highlands, to reconnect with each other, nature and parts of themselves they lost.

verdict.reason: A rare film about friendship and self-reckoning that earns its 130 minutes on foot through the Scottish Highlands. Schrijver trusts landscape and silence to do the emotional work.

ratings.plot: Two death-obsessed sisters, outcasts in their suburban neighborhood, must deal with the tragic consequences when one of them is bitten by a deadly werewolf.

verdict.reason: A smart horror film that uses genre to explore adolescent rage and female friendship. Fawcett's direction finds real darkly comic power in the werewolf setup.

ratings.plot: A determined taxi driver in Lagos forms an unexpected bond with a group of free-spirited women, leading her into a world of friendship and self-discovery despite the risks along the way.

verdict.reason: Olive Nwosu's debut feature earns a trip to Union Square for its sharp eye on Lagos life and female friendship. The 96-minute runtime lets the story breathe without overstaying.

ratings.plot: A sheltered and manipulative Southern belle and a roguish profiteer face off in a turbulent romance as the society around them crumbles with the end of slavery and is rebuilt during the Civil War and Reconstruction periods.

verdict.reason: Essential cinema history on the big screen after nearly a century. Fleming's scope and Technicolor sweep demand theatrical immersion over home viewing.

ratings.plot: A forgotten Peter Parker lives alone as a full-time Spider-Man until mounting pressure triggers a dangerous change and a powerful new enemy emerges.

verdict.reason: Cretton brings a sharp new angle to the character after the multiverse mess. The premise of a forgotten Peter forced into full-time vigilantism has real bite.

ratings.plot: Rescued from abandonment and raised by the King and Queen, Oedipus is still haunted by a prophecy--he'll murder his father and marry his mother.

verdict.reason: Pasolini's radical reading of Greek tragedy demands a theater screen. The DCP restoration at Metrograph makes this a rare chance to see how he remade myth into lived nightmare.

ratings.plot: After his mother's sudden death, Socrates, a 15-year-old living on the margins of São Paulo's coast, must survive on his own while coming to terms with his grief.

verdict.reason: A precise, unsentimental film about a teenager adrift after loss in São Paulo's margins. At 71 minutes, Moratto's direction cuts straight to the bone without wasting a frame.

ratings.plot: When Jonathan Harker rouses the ire of Count Dracula for accepting a job at the vampire's castle under false pretenses, his friend Dr. Van Helsing pursues the predatory villain.

verdict.reason: Fisher's 1958 vampire classic demands the big screen—the saturated Technicolor and sharp 35mm print at Metrograph make this essential. Lean 82 minutes of pure gothic atmosphere.

ratings.plot: The chief of a police unit that can accurately predict and prevent crimes goes on the run after he's accused of a future murder himself.

verdict.reason: Spielberg's 2002 thriller holds up as sharp sci-fi action with real ideas about power and guilt. Metrograph's DCP presentation makes the futuristic New York pop on the big screen.

ratings.plot: In 2004, an ad director faces a turbulent Christmas weekend. In 2026, a filmmaker turns her story into a screenplay, blurring the lines between reality, fiction, and the people closest to him.

verdict.reason: Almodóvar playing with reality and fiction across two decades deserves a big screen. The layering of autobiography and invention is exactly what this director does best.

ratings.plot: A teacher at an inner-city high school is convinced that his students have the potential to pass AP Calculus.

verdict.reason: A vital American film about teaching and belief that holds up completely. Edward James Olmos's performance and the classroom scenes have real power on the big screen.

ratings.plot: In 1870s high-society New York, a young lawyer falls for a woman separated from her husband while he's engaged to her cousin.

verdict.reason: Scorsese's formal mastery transforms Wharton into visual poetry on the big screen. Metrograph's 35mm print restores the film's lustrous cinematography to full depth.

ratings.plot: When the attempt to kill a professor goes wrong, a series of violent events are triggered which force a taxi driver to run for his life.

verdict.reason: Na Hong-jin's kinetic action thriller demands a theater. The DCP restoration at Metrograph makes this the right time to catch two hours of relentless pursuit and collision.

ratings.plot: Isolated from the rest of the world in their countryside mansion, an unhappily married couple engages in a series of increasingly violent role playing games in an effort to heal their relationship.

verdict.reason: Saura's 1969 film belongs in a theater, especially this restoration at Metrograph. The escalating games between the couple demand the intensity of a big screen.

ratings.plot: Harry's dead and, while no one really minds, everyone feels responsible. After Harry's body is found in the woods, several locals must determine not only how and why he was killed but what to do with the body.

verdict.reason: Hitchcock's rare comedy-mystery hybrid deserves the big screen. Metrograph's DCP restoration makes this 1955 gem sparkle with sharp dialogue and visual wit.

ratings.plot: A follow-up to Fede Alvarez's remake of Sam Raimi's 1981 film "The Evil Dead."

verdict.reason: Raimi's original sequel is a masterclass in horror-comedy on the big screen. The practical effects and slapstick timing demand theatrical sound and image.

ratings.plot: In October 1980, twenty environmental experts convene at a Florida hotel to draft a congressional statement on carbon dioxide emissions, but struggle to agree on the wording.

verdict.reason: Tom McCarthy finds comedy in the bureaucratic chaos of consensus-building among scientists. The specificity of a single October 1980 meeting gives the premise real dramatic weight.

ratings.plot: Feature-length version of the documentary TV series Planet Earth (2006), following the migration paths of four animal families.

verdict.reason: A rare 35mm theatrical screening of a visually stunning nature documentary. The migration sequences are built for big-screen immersion and Metrograph's print quality.

ratings.plot: When a machine that allows therapists to enter their patients' dreams is stolen, all hell breaks loose. Only a young female therapist, Paprika, can stop it.

ratings.plot: On July 27, 1986, Queen performed the largest-ever stadium concert at the Népstadion in Budapest in front of 80,000 ecstatic fans. Now, this original concert film has been beautifully rescanned and remastered in 4K alongside a dynamic new audio mix, featuring many of Queen's favorite tracks – "Bohemian Rhapsody," "Crazy Little Thing Called Love," "I Want To Break Free," and "We Are The Champions." With three years to go before the fall of the Berlin Wall, this was the first Western rock concert performed in a stadium behind the then-Iron Curtain. It was of such significance to the Hungarian authorities and film industry that a group of the country's top film cameramen and technicians were brought together to film it for posterity.

verdict.reason: The 4K restoration of Queen's final tour with Freddie Mercury deserves the big screen and pristine sound. This is a historical document of a breakthrough moment—the first major Western rock concert behind the Iron Curtain—shot by Hungary's best cinematographers and now given the restoration it earned.

movies.title: Alamo Drafthouse x A24 Cinema Club: Pearl

ratings.plot: The allure of stardom on the big screen proves to be a road to some very dark places for Mia Goth’s titular PEARL in this stylish and gruesome prequel to Ti West’s X. With her husband away at war, Pearl finds herself dreaming of a way to escape from her boring life on the farm. She sees the silver screen as her way to find stardom and the love she so desperately needs, but her overbearing mother and her own dark impulses might hold her back from the fame she craves. PEARL proves to be a delightfully perverse study on a standout character from writer/director Ti West’s tribute to ‘70s grindhouse, X. Its vibrant, candy-coated veneer plays wonderfully against the depraved desires of the main character bubbling just below the surface. Co-writer/star Mia Goth gives another deliciously unhinged performance as Pearl, a not-quite-innocent farm girl looking for love in all the wrong places. As much a love letter to the Golden Age of Hollywood as it is a demented look at the darkness bubbling just below the surface of rural America, PEARL is colorful, unnerving, and twisted in all the right ways.

verdict.reason: Ti West's prequel is a stylish, unhinged descent into obsession and rage. Mia Goth's performance and the film's candy-colored dread make it essential theater.

ratings.plot: One of the most derided movies of the 20th century is also one of its most spectacularly misunderstood. The odd-couple tag team of Dutch provocateur director Paul Verhoeven (ROBOCOP, ELLE) and Sleazoid-Hungarian-American writer Joe Eszterhas (FLASHDANCE, SLIVER) first came together with 1992's BASIC INSTINCT, and everyone, including the financial backers and the producer/distributors of this movie, assumed lightning would strike twice for the duo with 1995's SHOWGIRLS. Universally panned by critics upon its initial release, people found the multi-tap combo of inane dialogue, wild over-acting, and extreme obscenity and grotesquerie to be just too much. Then the "so-bad-it's-good" crowd sunk their hollow claws into the movie, claiming it as one of the "best worst" movies of all time. To be sure, yes, this is a movie in which Saved By the Bell 's Elizabeth Berkley sets fire to her TV-star image by grinding her pelvis on Kyle MacLachlan's lap until he simulates sexual climax while Gina Gershon watches. She shoves chips into her mouth and reminisces about her days of eating and enjoying "puppy chow," between bouts of trying to make it as a Las Vegas showgirl "goddess." The assumption that critics and chuckleheads alike have made are that a) Verhoeven and Eszterhas weren't trying to make something with humor (they were), and b) that the surface story is meant to be taken at face value (it's not). Verhoemie don't play that. SHOWGIRLS is a complicated, satirical masterpiece that tests the audience's limits of empathy and challenges some basic assumptions about American dreams of celebrity, pokes at the artificiality of Hollywood glitz and glamour, and shines a light on the misogyny and dehumanization inherent in the entertainment industry, all while keeping the audiences on their toes as they try to know whether they should laugh, cry, or scratch their heads because there are random interruptions by chimpanzees and the fiercest dancing ever committed to celluloid. (Laird Jimenez)

verdict.reason: Verhoeven's satire on Hollywood misogyny deserves a room full of people who get the joke. The book club format transforms a notorious film into a communal event worth the trip.

It’s Austen by way of a modern romantic comedy, where money is tight, feelings are tighter, and “I greatly esteem him” is Regency-speak for “I have it bad for this man.” Sisterly solidarity, social maneuvering, and romantic complications are all on the menu.

ratings.plot: At Chester’s cottage, good behavior earns karaoke. Getting answers is a little more complicated. After a mysterious apocalyptic(ish) attack leaves them bloodied, disoriented, and unable to speak, Liam (Joey Bader) and Mel (Kaylee McGregor) take refuge in the English countryside. Their oddball host, Chester (Oliver Woolf), feeds them, helps them recover, and introduces a system of rewards: behave yourself, earn “nifties,” cash them in for hot-tub time and dance parties. Beyond the cottage, things are less nifty. But within it, a makeshift family is taking shape. While Liam embraces their new life, Mel grows increasingly curious about the world Chester insists is too dangerous to enter… In their feature debut, directors Scott Tinkham and Michael Woloson mix deadpan comedy, sibling rivalry, and creeping unease in a coming-of-age story about people who have to grow up all over again. Winner of the Special Jury Prize at the 2026 Manchester Film Festival and the Narrative Feature Audience Award at Dances With Films LA 2026, this has the sort of sensibilities that fans of Yorgos Lanthimos and Ben Wheatley will adore… and it’s a natural fit as an Alamo Exclusive.

verdict.reason: Feature debut mixing deadpan comedy and creeping unease with real formal ambition. Alamo Exclusive screened early—catch it before word spreads and the midnight crowds arrive.

ratings.plot: Where would we be without PSYCHO? Sixty years on and Hitchcock’s delicious cod-Freudian nightmare about a platinum-blonde embezzler (Janet Leigh) who neglected to consult a guide before selecting her motel still has much to answer for. It blazed a bloody trail for the much-loved slasher cycle, but it also assured us that a B-movie could be A-grade in quality and innovation. It dared to suggest that your star didn’t need to surface from an ordeal smelling of roses (or, indeed, at all). It combined a knife, a scream, a melon, some chocolate sauce, Bernard Herrmann’s greatest score, and more than 70 edits to push the envelope of screen violence. It lent The Simpsons some of its best gags. It offers perfect case studies of suspense, paranoia, and montage for lazy film studies tutors. And, of course, it was the first movie to show a toilet flushing, so we might also credit it with spawning the entire gross-out genre. PSYCHO: We salute you. (David Jenkins, Time Out )

verdict.reason: See Hitchcock's masterpiece on the big screen at no cost; a rare gift. The 70+ cuts in that shower scene still reshape how violence reads in cinema.

ratings.plot: It is difficult to imagine precisely what cinema would be without its most influential and memorable titles. THE CABINET OF DR. CALIGARI in particular stands out as one such notable title in the international canon that in its time and forever thereafter has been heralded as a masterpiece of its craft, the singular model for expressionist, black-and-white filmmaking. A landmark of horror filmmaking, its visual style is often copied or paid homage, and its remarkable twist ending has become all but a modern trope. Its long, haunting shadows and canted, dreamlike production design stay with viewers weeks, months, and years following an initial viewing. The film is credited for introducing the "twist" ending and inspired EDWARD SCISSORHANDS by Tim Burton, THE IMAGINARIUM OF DR. PARNASSUS by Terry Gilliam, and Martin Scorsese's SHUTTER ISLAND, all of which share many striking similarities to CALIGARI. "The first thing everyone notices and best remembers about THE CABINET OF DR. CALIGARI (1920) is the film's bizarre look. The actors inhabit a jagged landscape of sharp angles and tilted walls and windows, staircases climbing crazy diagonals, trees with spiky leaves, grass that looks like knives. These radical distortions immediately set the film apart from all earlier ones." – Roger Ebert, Chicago Sun-Times

verdict.reason: See the expressionist blueprint on the big screen with live music. The jagged set design and canted angles demand theatrical scale.
